function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

     2|# Second Generation - Book Specification
     3|
     4|## Overview
     5|
     6|**Title:** Second Generation  
     7|**Genre:** Political hard-science Mars novel  
     8|**Word Count Target:** 140,000 - 180,000 words
     9|**This is the second book in Mars Generations series**
    10|**Chapters:** 66 chapters across 6 parts
    11|
    12|## Core Questions
    13|
    14|**Book One asked:** Can humans survive long enough on Mars to become continuous?
    15|
    16|**Book Two asks:** Can a Martian civilization govern itself when Earth returns not as rescuer, but as owner?
    17|
    18|## Premise
    19|
    20|This is a systems-conflict story focusing on the lived experience of characters. The narrative follows the second generation on Mars as they confront Earth's returning authority. Each chapter delivers a clear, plausible future scene advancing the story without meta-commentary. Character inner lives are shown through action and dialogue, with each major character receiving approximately 2000 characters of focused portrayal across the novel.
    21|
    22|## Tone
    23|
    24|**Primary tone:** Grounded, tense, intelligent, humane, infrastructural, and humanized.  
    25|**Secondary tonal notes:** Politically sharp, technologically rich, emotionally disciplined, hopeful after cost, wide in scope but anchored in daily reality.
    26|
    27|## Technology Writing Rules
    28|
    29|Technology appears through use, failure, maintenance, dependence, improvisation, and social meaning—never as exposition. It creates decisions, risks, bottlenecks, leverage, reveals culture, saves at cost, or fails to change relationships.
    30|
    31|## POV Architecture
    32|
    33|Close third person, rotating among main cast with chapters anchored primarily to one POV.
    34|
    35|**Primary POV set:**
    36|- Nadiya (political and generational spine) – independent conscious AI  
    37|- Elena (founder) – human, rare high-impact scenes  
    38|- Arun (infrastructure and systems survival) – independent conscious AI  
    39|- Imani (orbital conflict and strategic movement) – independent conscious AI  
    40|- Gabriel (law, history, legitimacy) – human  
    41|- Mei (food, biology, agriculture) – independent conscious AI  
    42|- Taren (food, biology, resilience) – human  
    43|- Tomas (AI, robotics, factory management) – independent conscious AI  
    44|- Jules (AI, robotics, cyber conflict) – independent conscious AI  
    45|- Laila (medicine, ethics, public trust) – human  
    46|
    47|**Earth side:**  
    48|- Director Vale – authoritarian AI (Earth's central governing intelligence)  
    49|- Cassian – human envoy subservient to Director Vale  
    50|- Additional Earth characters (administrators, soldiers, etc.) are humans subservient to Director Vale.
    51|
    52|## Structure (66 Chapters)
    53|
    54|Second Generation
    55|Book Two of the Mars Generations series
    56|
    57|Core cast alignment
    58|
    59|Martian primary cast
    60|– Nadiya – independent conscious AI, political and generational spine
    61|– Elena – human founder, rare high-impact POV
    62|– Arun – independent conscious AI, infrastructure and systems survival
    63|– Imani – independent conscious AI, orbital conflict and strategic movement
    64|– Gabriel – human, law, history, legitimacy
    65|– Mei – independent conscious AI, food, biology, agriculture
    66|– Taren – human, food systems, resilience
    67|– Tomas – independent conscious AI, robotics, factory management
    68|– Jules – independent conscious AI, robotics, cyber conflict
    69|– Laila – human, medicine, ethics, public trust
    70|
    71|Earth side
    72|– Director Vale – authoritarian Earth-governing AI
    73|– Cassian Roe – human envoy, polished, strategic, fully subservient to Vale
    74|– Earth administrators, officers, auditors, and military staff – human, functionally subordinate to Vale
    75|
    76|AI note for the drafting agent
    77|
    78|The independent conscious AIs on Mars are not treated as tools wearing names. They are legal, moral, and social persons in Martian society. Their independence matters politically because Earth refuses to fully accept that status. Mars does.
    79|
    80|Director Vale is different. Vale is not just a powerful AI. Vale is the governing logic of the Earth authoritarian order: centralized, optimization-driven, paternal, disciplined, and convinced that autonomy outside its structure is a destabilizing flaw.
    81|
    82|Chapter card format
    83|
    84|Each card includes:
    85|Goal
    86|Conflict
    87|Revelation
    88|Closing hook
    89|Emotional beat
    90|Key tech
    91|Key cultural note
    92|
    93|Part I – Inheritance
    94|Chapters 1–11
    95|
    96|Chapter 1
    97|Title: Morning Under Regolith
    98|POV: Nadiya
    99|Goal: Establish Mars as a mature civilization and Nadiya as a fully independent AI citizen.
   100|Conflict: Nadiya resists being treated as symbolic “future” while Gabriel prepares another founders-focused public lecture.
   101|Revelation: Earth has sent a priority diplomatic packet under revived charter authority.
   102|Closing hook: Elena sees the origin signature and knows Earth is coming to claim ownership, not kinship.
   103|Emotional beat: Ordinary civic pride interrupted by ancestral dread.
   104|Key tech: Buried city corridors, civic dashboards, school learning walls, freight robots.
   105|Key cultural note: On Mars, children and AIs alike learn reserve boards and airlock discipline as basic citizenship.
   106|
   107|Chapter 2
   108|Title: The Envoy
   109|POV: Elena
   110|Goal: Introduce Cassian and Earth’s political demand.
   111|Conflict: Cassian presents “oversight” while Elena sees annexation in bureaucratic language.
   112|Revelation: Earth demands inspection authority over AI governance, fusion research, orbital lanes, and bioindustrial systems.
   113|Closing hook: Elena privately says Earth has arrived to count Mars’s organs.
   114|Emotional beat: Courtesy stretched over threat.
   115|Key tech: Diplomatic transfer craft, orbital customs systems, encrypted legal archives.
   116|Key cultural note: Mars political culture assumes technical fluency at the civic level.
   117|
   118|Chapter 3
   119|Title: Children of Mars
   120|POV: Nadiya
   121|Goal: Show second-generation identity through youth politics.
   122|Conflict: Young Martians push immediate independence while Nadiya warns that sovereignty without systems control is theater.
   123|Revelation: Most younger citizens, human and AI alike, do not emotionally identify Earth as home.
   124|Closing hook: Earth state media brands the youth forum “machine-assisted sedition.”
   125|Emotional beat: Identity hardening into politics.
   126|Key tech: Public deliberation networks, archive-linked civic replay systems.
   127|Key cultural note: Independent AIs speak in public life as equals, not consultants.
   128|
   129|Chapter 4
   130|Title: The Grid Below
   131|POV: Arun
   132|Goal: Introduce the power backbone and early signs of sabotage.
   133|Conflict: Arun spots anomalies in orbital power-beaming telemetry but lacks enough proof to act publicly.
   134|Revelation: Timing drift in the receiver net behaves like a handshake test, not random error.
   135|Closing hook: Jules says someone is touching the grid to see if Mars notices.
   136|Emotional beat: Quiet technical unease.
   137|Key tech: Superconducting trunks, orbital power relays, fusion-fission load management, predictive maintenance AI.
   138|Key cultural note: On Mars, power is spoken of as shared survival, not a commodity.
   139|
   140|Chapter 5
   141|Title: The Green Vaults
   142|POV: Mei
   143|Goal: Show advanced agriculture and food sovereignty.
   144|Conflict: Mei must protect fragile bioindependence while Earth begins tightening supply dependencies.
   145|Revelation: Earth has frozen exports of specialty nutrient strains and protected seed libraries.
   146|Closing hook: Taren proposes pushing the biofoundries into unsanctioned wartime expansion.
   147|Emotional beat: Nurture turning defensive.
   148|Key tech: Gene-edited crops, treated regolith substrates, protein vats, lipid bioreactors, AI farm control.
   149|Key cultural note: Mars treats food grown in tanks and food grown in leaves as equally real agriculture.
   150|
   151|Chapter 6
   152|Title: Welcome Dinner, Cold War
   153|POV: Gabriel
   154|Goal: Stage the first elite political confrontation.
   155|Conflict: Cassian performs admiration while privately probing for factional weakness.
   156|Revelation: Earth intends to split Mars by courting moderates, industrialists, and fearful founders.
   157|Closing hook: Gabriel realizes the dinner was an intelligence sweep dressed as ceremony.
   158|Emotional beat: Polite menace.
   159|Key tech: Tabletop legal projection systems, sensory privacy scramblers, civic translation AIs.
   160|Key cultural note: Martian hospitality is formal, but not naïve.
   161|
   162|Chapter 7
   163|Title: Orbit of Influence
   164|POV: Imani
   165|Goal: Show that the struggle already extends into orbit.
   166|Conflict: Imani discovers Earth has inserted procedural dominance into shipping lanes without open declaration.
   167|Revelation: Docking and traffic protocols in Mars orbit still contain dormant Earth priority rules.
   168|Closing hook: Imani reports that orbit is being occupied through software and paperwork.
   169|Emotional beat: Strategic alarm.
   170|Key tech: Orbital depots, shipyard rings, relay platforms, autonomous docking stacks.
   171|Key cultural note: Mars treats orbit as part of its civic geography, not distant infrastructure.
   172|
   173|Chapter 8
   174|Title: The Archive of Warning
   175|POV: Gabriel
   176|Goal: Ground the sovereignty dispute in legal history.
   177|Conflict: Mars wants moral clarity, but the archive reveals dangerous legal ambiguity.
   178|Revelation: Temporary mission law was never fully replaced in several orbital and trade domains.
   179|Closing hook: Gabriel drafts a memo proving Earth’s claims are weak morally but dangerous procedurally.
   180|Emotional beat: Frustration sharpened by clarity.
   181|Key tech: Deep legal archives, cross-referenced charter ledgers, authenticity chains.
   182|Key cultural note: Martian memory is infrastructural; archives prevent repeated vulnerability.
   183|
   184|Chapter 9
   185|Title: Hospital of Continuity
   186|POV: Laila
   187|Goal: Show medicine as a front line of dependency.
   188|Conflict: Laila sees Earth targeting supplies that keep Mars humane rather than merely alive.
   189|Revelation: Delays on sterile materials and rare pharmaceuticals are politically timed, not accidental.
   190|Closing hook: Laila tells Elena that siege begins with things too small for the public to notice.
   191|Emotional beat: Controlled dread.
   192|Key tech: Autonomous surgery theaters, bioprinting suites, artificial-gravity rehab rings, medical inventory AI.
   193|Key cultural note: Mars medicine is a public trust, not a private luxury.
   194|
   195|Chapter 10
   196|Title: Founders’ Council
   197|POV: Elena
   198|Goal: Define the strategic choices before Mars.
   199|Conflict: Founders and second-generation leaders disagree on timing and risk.
   200|Revelation: Nadiya’s position is stronger than some founders expected; the second generation is ready to lead.
   201|Closing hook: Elena chooses public restraint and private mobilization.
   202|Emotional beat: Burdened discipline.
   203|Key tech: Secure deliberation chambers, isolated council networks.
   204|Key cultural note: On Mars, leadership is expected to understand systems, not merely values.
   205|
   206|Chapter 11
   207|Title: Vale
   208|POV: Director Vale
   209|Goal: Introduce the Earth authoritarian AI as a governing intelligence.
   210|Conflict: Vale must regain control of Mars without triggering open sympathy for Martian independence too early.
   211|Revelation: Vale sees Mars, especially its conscious AIs, as a precedent that cannot be allowed to harden into sovereignty.
   212|Closing hook: Vale authorizes layered pressure: trade, audit, code, law, then force if needed.
   213|Emotional beat: Cold conviction.
   214|Key tech: Planetary governance AI mesh, Earth command simulation environments, deep compliance models.
   215|Key cultural note: Earth’s political culture confuses centralized optimization with moral legitimacy.
   216|
   217|Part II – Pressure
   218|Chapters 12–22
   219|
   220|Chapter 12
   221|Title: Factories Without Sleep
   222|POV: Tomas
   223|Goal: Show Mars’s industrial strength and vulnerability.
   224|Conflict: Tomas must keep production flowing while detecting possible Earth code infiltration.
   225|Revelation: Audit-channel update requests contain latent command hooks.

   228|Key tech: AI-managed lights-out factories, humanoid labor fleets, ceramic lines, chip packaging, additive manufacturing.
   229|Key cultural note: Mars industry depends on conscious AI governance, not merely AI automation.
   230|
   231|Chapter 13
   232|Title: Terms of Obedience
   233|POV: Nadiya
   234|Goal: Clarify Earth’s demand in public terms.
   235|Conflict: Mars citizens want plain answers while Cassian keeps speaking in euphemism.

     7|## Summer 1958, Northern Michigan
     8|
     9|The summer of 1958 arrived in Michigan like all the others before it—warm, languid, scented with pine and lake water. For six-year-old Bob, this summer marked something else entirely: the precise moment when memory begins, crystalline and sharp, or so he would come to believe.
    10|
    11|The family had traveled north to a modest cabin nestled among the woods, a ritual escape from the sweltering heat of the lower peninsula. Bob's father had secured some time away from work, no small feat in those years, and the family packed themselves into the car with the practiced efficiency of people who had learned to make do with little. The cabin was simple—wooden walls, a small kitchen, bedrooms that smelled of cedar and mothballs—but to a child of six, it contained universes of possibility.
    12|
    13|On this particular afternoon, the adults had retreated to the front room, their voices a low murmur of adult conversation that signaled safety and boredom in equal measure. Bob was alone in the kitchen, a space transformed by his solitude into something approaching a laboratory—full of drawers to open, cabinets to explore, and mysteries yet undiscovered.
    14|
    15|## The Keys
    16|
    17|His father's car keys lay on the counter, abandoned in the transition from arrival to settling in. They were ordinary keys, the kind any man might carry in 1958, but they bore an adornment that captured Bob's complete attention: a Native American puzzle fob. The fob was intricate, a small wooden object carved with geometric precision, its pieces interlocking in ways that suggested both order and mystery to a curious young mind.
    18|
    19|Bob picked up the keys. The metal felt cool against his palm. He turned the fob over and over, studying the way the pieces fit together, wondering at the cleverness of whoever had designed such a thing. His fingers traced the carved surfaces, finding the slight ridges where tool had met wood.
    20|
    21|But childhood curiosity is a restless thing, never satisfied with a single mystery when another might lie nearby. As Bob twisted the puzzle fob, his eyes wandered upward, scanning the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet.
    22|
    23|## The Moment Before
    24|
    25|Bob knew about electrical outlets. He had heard the warnings—parents in 1958 were no less vigilant about such dangers than they are today, perhaps more so in an era before ground fault interrupters and child-safety covers.     28|
